blocks.text: The GitHub MCP server turns your GitHub account into a set of tools an agent can call directly.
Instead of copying an issue or a diff into a chat window, an agent asks for it and gets structured data back.
This lesson covers what it exposes, how you authenticate, and a real triage workflow you can build on.
1. What Is the GitHub MCP Server

blocks.alt: What Is the GitHub MCP Server
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441589930-754361337.png
The GitHub MCP server is an official server maintained by GitHub that speaks the Model Context Protocol.
It sits between an agent and the GitHub API, translating tool calls into real GitHub operations.
Any MCP capable client, a coding assistant, a chat app, or your own agent, can plug it in the same way.
It ships both as an npm package and as a container image, so you can run it locally or in a hosted setup.
Under the hood it calls the same GitHub REST API you would call yourself, just wrapped in MCP tools.
2. Resources: Repositories, Issues, and Pull Requests as Data
Resources are the read side of the server, the data an agent can pull in as context before deciding anything.

items: Repository metadata, such as description, default branch, and topics
Issue threads, including title, body, labels, and comments
Pull request details, including status, reviewers, and the diff itself
Commit history for a branch or a pull request

blocks.text: An agent typically reads several of these before it writes anything back to GitHub.

blocks.title: Resources are read only
blocks.content: Nothing an agent does with a resource changes GitHub. Only a tool call can create, comment, or merge.

blocks.text: 3. Tools the GitHub MCP Server Exposes
Tools are the write side, the actions an agent can trigger once it understands the situation.
Each tool takes a small set of named arguments, similar to calling a function with keyword parameters.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Tool","What It Does"],"rows":[["get_issue","Fetches the title, body, labels, and status of one issue"],["create_issue","Opens a new issue with a title, body, and labels"],["list_issues","Lists issues in a repository, filterable by state and label"],["add_issue_comment","Posts a comment on an existing issue"],["get_pull_request","Fetches metadata for a pull request"],["get_pull_request_diff","Returns the actual code changes in a pull request"],["list_commits","Lists commits on a branch or a pull request"],["create_pull_request_review","Submits a review with comments on a pull request"]]}

blocks.text: The exact tool names can vary slightly by server version, but this set covers the common core.
4. Creating an Issue With a Tool Call

blocks.alt: Creating an Issue With a Tool Call
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441589930-474971656.png
Creating an issue is one of the simplest and most common actions an agent takes on GitHub.
The owner and repo fields tell the server exactly where to create the issue.
The response includes the new issue number and its URL, so the agent can reference it right away.
5. Reading a Pull Request Diff
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441589931-671407351.png
Before an agent can review or summarize a pull request, it needs the actual code changes.
The response comes back as a plain diff, the same format you would see in a terminal.
For a very large pull request, ask the agent to summarize file by file instead of the whole diff at once.
6. Listing Commits on a Branch
Commit history helps an agent understand what changed recently and who changed it.
This is useful for questions like, has anyone touched this file since the last release.
Results are paginated, so a busy repository may need a few calls with an increasing page number.
7. Authenticating With a Personal Access Token

blocks.alt: Authenticating With a Personal Access Token
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441589931-388667189.png
The simplest way to authenticate is a personal access token, stored as an environment variable.
A fine grained token scoped to just the repositories your agent needs is the safer choice.

blocks.title: Keep tokens out of source control
blocks.content: Store the token in an environment variable or a secrets manager, never hardcoded in a config file you commit.

items: Open GitHub settings and choose Developer settings, then Fine grained tokens
Pick the exact repositories the agent should be able to reach
Grant only the permissions it needs, such as Issues and Pull requests

blocks.text: 8. Authenticating With OAuth
OAuth suits multi user setups, where a hosted agent acts on behalf of many different GitHub accounts.
The user approves access through GitHub, and the server exchanges that approval for a short lived token.
This avoids handing out long lived personal tokens to every user of a shared agent.
The token GitHub issues through OAuth also expires and refreshes, which limits the damage if it ever leaks.
9. Configuring the Server in Your MCP Client
Most MCP clients read a config file that lists which servers to start and how to reach them.
Restart the client after editing this file so it picks up the new server entry.
9.1 Local Versus Hosted Servers
Running the server locally over stdio is simplest for a single developer on their own machine.
A hosted deployment behind HTTP suits a team, since many users can share one running server.
10. A Practical Agent Workflow: Triaging New Issues

blocks.alt: A Practical Agent Workflow: Triaging New Issues
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441589931-639769246.png
A triage agent watches for new issues and gives each one a first pass before a human sees it.
The steps below use only the resources and tools already covered in this lesson.

items: List open issues that do not yet have a label
Fetch the full body and any linked pull requests for each one
Decide on a category, such as bug, question, or feature request
Apply labels and post a short comment summarizing the next step

blocks.text: 11. Reading Context Before Taking Action
A good triage agent reads before it writes, checking existing labels, linked issues, and recent commits.
Skipping this step leads to duplicate labels, contradictory comments, and confused maintainers.

items: Check whether the issue already has labels before adding new ones
Look for linked or duplicate issues in the same repository
Glance at recent commits to see if the bug was already fixed

blocks.text: 12. Guardrails and Scoped Permissions
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441589932-295298522.png
An agent with write access to GitHub can cause real damage if it is given too much freedom too fast.

items: Scope the token to only the repositories the agent actually needs
Start in a read only mode before granting write tools
Require a human review step for closing issues or merging pull requests
Log every tool call so actions can be audited later

blocks.title: Watch your rate limits
blocks.content: The GitHub API caps how many requests you can make per hour, so a busy triage agent should batch its calls.

blocks.text: 13. Combining the GitHub Server With Other MCP Servers

blocks.alt: Combining the GitHub Server With Other MCP Servers
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441589932-873697903.png
The GitHub server is rarely used alone in a real workflow.
Pair it with a Slack server to post triage summaries, or a Linear server to mirror issues into a roadmap.

items: GitHub server plus Slack server, to post a daily triage digest
GitHub server plus a calendar server, to schedule a review meeting for a big pull request
GitHub server plus a documentation server, to check if docs need updating alongside code

blocks.text: 14. Worked Example
Say a new issue titled Login page throws 500 on empty password just came in with no labels.
The agent walks through the same four tools covered earlier in this lesson, in a natural order.

code.content:
1. list_issues   owner=your-org repo=your-repo state=open label=none
2. get_issue     owner=your-org repo=your-repo issueNumber=531
3. list_commits  owner=your-org repo=your-repo sha=main perPage=5
4. add_issue_comment owner=your-org repo=your-repo issueNumber=531
   body="Thanks for the report. Tagging this as a bug for the backend team."

blocks.text: The agent reads the issue, checks recent commits for related changes, then labels and comments in one pass.
A maintainer opens their inbox to an issue that is already sorted, summarized, and pointed at the right team.
None of this required a human to open GitHub, yet a human still decides whether to actually fix the bug.
15. Common Mistakes

items: Granting a token full account access when repo scoped access would do
Letting an agent close or merge without any human checkpoint
Skipping the diff and summarizing a pull request from its title alone
Forgetting to restart the MCP client after changing the config file
Reusing one shared token across many users instead of using OAuth

blocks.text: 16. Practice
Connect the GitHub MCP server to a test repository using a personal access token scoped to just that repo.
Write an agent prompt that lists open unlabeled issues, then have it label and comment on just one.
Read a real pull request diff through the server and ask the agent to summarize the change in three sentences.

items: Beginner: connect the server and list open issues in one repository
Intermediate: build the full triage flow from the worked example above
Advanced: add a guardrail so the agent asks before applying any label it has not used before

blocks.text: 17. Key Takeaway
The GitHub MCP server gives an agent read access to repositories, issues, and pull requests, plus tools to act on them.
Scope tokens tightly, keep a human in the loop for risky actions, and let the agent handle the repetitive triage work.
Once triage feels reliable, the same pattern extends naturally to reviewing diffs and drafting release notes.
